title: Integrals: area under a curve
summary: An integral adds up thin slices. Integrating a spectrum over wavelength gives a total power or a total number of photons. Rectangles and ∫x dx are all you need.

diagrams.title: Adding up slices of a spectrum
diagrams.tryThis: Increase the number of slices from 4 to 100 and watch the rectangle sum approach the exact area; then move the limits to integrate only part of the spectrum.

checks.prompt: A spectrum is constant at 0.5 W m⁻² nm⁻¹ between 400 nm and 1000 nm, and zero elsewhere. What is the irradiance?
hints: Area of a rectangle = height × width.
The antiderivative of x is x²/2.
solution: Geometrically: a trapezoid with parallel sides 1 and 3 and width 2: area (1 + 3)/2 × 2 = 4.

checks.prompt: $I_{e\lambda}$ is in W m⁻² nm⁻¹ and λ in nm. What is the unit of $\int I_{e\lambda}\,\mathrm{d}\lambda$?

options.feedback: Correct: the integral multiplies the y-unit by the x-unit, so nm⁻¹ × nm cancels.
Integrating over λ multiplies by the unit of dλ (nm), which cancels the nm⁻¹.
The units multiply, they don’t divide: nm⁻¹ × nm = 1.
There is no time integral here; the result is still a power per area.

hints: An integral is a sum of (height × width) slices.
Unit of the result = unit of y × unit of x.
solution: Each slice contributes $I_{e\lambda}\,\mathrm{d}\lambda$: (W m⁻² nm⁻¹) × nm = W m⁻².
That is why the area under a spectrum is an irradiance.
